s-fb1-high-0.essay:
When people argue about the four-day school week, they usually argue about Fridays. Teachers and teenagers picture a three-day weekend, and working parents picture a day-care bill. But the real question for a district isn't whether Fridays off are good or bad. It's who ends up paying for them. A district should move to a four-day week only if it will do two things before the first Thursday dismissal: lengthen the remaining days enough to keep total instructional hours the same, and pay for a Friday option for children under twelve. If it can't afford both, it should find another way to fix its teacher shortage.

The case for the schedule is not really about money, even though money is what gets announced. Harrow Fork saved about $410,000, "close to 2 percent of its operating budget" (Source A), and Source D found that savings across 23 districts topped out at 2.5 percent, with none reaching the 5 percent some had promised. Source F shows why. The biggest savings come from parking buses ($165,000) and paying for fewer utilities, and there is no bar for teacher salaries at all, because teachers get paid the same whether school meets four days or five. A district hoping to balance its budget this way will be disappointed. What it can realistically buy is teachers. Harrow Fork went from 14 unfilled positions to 5 (Source A), Pinemont Valley's science posting went from two applications to eleven (Source C), and across the Meridian Basin applicants per vacancy rose 2.4 times (Source D). That is the same pattern at the scale of one job, one district, and a whole region, which makes it hard to dismiss as luck. For a rural district that can't find a science teacher, this is a serious argument.

The problem is that the hiring benefit goes to the district while the cost goes somewhere else. Marisol Ettinger, a store owner with two kids in elementary school, pays $76 a week, over $2,700 a year, for Friday care, and she argues that "a saving that moves from the district's ledger to mine is not a saving; it is a transfer" (Source B). It would be easy to write her off as one frustrated parent, except that Source D found 41 percent of parents of children under 12 reported new childcare costs and 22 percent cut their own work hours. Source E shows the same split: 84 percent of teachers want to keep the calendar, but elementary parents are divided 48 to 42, and local employers, probably the people covering for those parents' missing hours, oppose it 49 to 37. The groups who like the schedule most are the ones it was designed to help, and the people closest to the youngest children are the ones paying for it.

That is why the conditions matter. Source D's achievement findings suggest the four-day schedule isn't the problem; lost hours are. Districts that kept total hours saw growth "statistically indistinguishable" from five-day districts, while those that cut hours fell 3 percentile points behind in math, mostly in grades 2 through 5. Pinemont Valley's third and fourth graders slipped in reading the first year, and the gap only closed after the district moved reading to the morning and paid for Friday tutoring (Source C). So a first-year dip doesn't prove the schedule fails, but a closed gap doesn't prove it works by itself either. Castellane's own summary, "We got lucky, and then we worked," reads less like a success story than a warning.

Even Pinemont hasn't solved childcare. Its enrichment day serves about 140 children at two of five buildings, paid for mostly by a county grant, and Castellane tells critics to "ask to see the waiting list." A district without that grant is not Pinemont. Harrow Fork has a library turning children away on Fridays and day-cares adding new rates, which suggests the town absorbed the cost instead of the district planning for it. Before a board copies Pinemont's results, it should ask whether it can copy Pinemont's repair work.

The four-day week is not a budget fix, and it is not a gift. It's a trade: teachers in exchange for a Friday that someone has to cover. A district that pays for that Friday itself has made a fair trade. A district that can't should take Source B's advice, raise the levy and pay teachers directly, because at least that puts the cost where everyone can see it.

annotations.comment: This conditional thesis earns the point because it names specific conditions instead of saying 'it depends.' It also sets up the line of reasoning the essay follows: what the district gains, who pays for it, and why each condition is needed.

annotations.quote: If it can't afford both, it should find another way to fix its teacher shortage.
annotations.comment: The thesis also says what happens if the conditions aren't met, so it commits to a stance. The conclusion picks this up again with the levy alternative.

annotations.quote: Source F shows why. The biggest savings come from parking buses ($165,000) and paying for fewer utilities, and there is no bar for teacher salaries at all
annotations.comment: This interprets the chart instead of just repeating it. The missing salary bar explains why savings stay near 2 percent, and the writer connects Source F to the figures in Sources A and D.

annotations.quote: That is the same pattern at the scale of one job, one district, and a whole region, which makes it hard to dismiss as luck.
annotations.comment: This is synthesis, not stacking: Sources A, C, and D are read as the same effect at three scales. That lets the writer say the hiring benefit is the real case for the schedule.

annotations.quote: It would be easy to write her off as one frustrated parent, except that Source D found 41 percent of parents of children under 12 reported new childcare costs
annotations.comment: The writer uses Source D's survey data to show that Source B's single story reflects a wider pattern. Two sources are put in conversation here.

annotations.quote: local employers, probably the people covering for those parents' missing hours, oppose it 49 to 37
annotations.comment: The Source E numbers are interpreted, not just reproduced. The writer offers a reason the employer row differs from the teacher row and ties the gap to the essay's point about who pays.

annotations.quote: Source D's achievement findings suggest the four-day schedule isn't the problem; lost hours are.
annotations.comment: This reads Source D accurately: it does not claim four-day weeks raise scores. It then uses Source C's reading data to support the first condition in the thesis, which addresses evidence that cuts against adopting the schedule.

annotations.quote: So a first-year dip doesn't prove the schedule fails, but a closed gap doesn't prove it works by itself either.
annotations.comment: The essay separates short-run effects from long-run ones and explains why neither settles the question alone. This is one of the complex moves the rubric lists.

annotations.quote: A district without that grant is not Pinemont.
annotations.comment: The writer asks whether one district's results transfer to another and builds on that question through the next sentences about Harrow Fork. Treating Pinemont and Harrow Fork as different districts is another move the rubric names.

annotations.quote: It's a trade: teachers in exchange for a Friday that someone has to cover.
annotations.comment: The question of who gains and who pays runs from the opening paragraph to this conclusion and drives the whole decision. That is why the sophistication is sustained, not a single sentence. The vivid, plain style ('a day-care bill,' 'the lunch line' idea) also strengthens the argument.

s-fb1-mid-0.essay:
A school district should only move to a four-day week if it is willing to keep the same number of instructional hours and provide care for families on Fridays. Without those two things, the schedule saves a little money but costs students and parents too much.

The main reason districts do this is money and teachers, and the sources show both benefits are real but small or uneven. In Source A, Harrow Fork saved about 410,000 dollars, which is close to 2 percent of its budget. Source F shows that most of this came from transportation and utilities, and none of it came from teacher salaries. That means the savings are not very big, since salaries are the biggest cost. Source D agrees, saying no district reached the 5 percent that some expected. So if a district is only doing this to save money, it is probably not worth it.

The better argument for the four-day week is hiring teachers. Source A says Harrow Fork went from 14 unfilled positions to 5, and Source C says Pinemont Valley got eleven applicants for a job that used to get two. Source D also found that four-day districts had 2.4 times as many applicants. These all show that teachers like the schedule, which is also shown in Source E where 84 percent of teachers want to keep it. This is a strong point in favor of the schedule, because a district with empty classrooms has a serious problem.

However, the schedule has real downsides for younger kids and for families. Source D says districts that cut total hours had math scores that fell behind by 3 percentile points, especially in grades 2 through 5. Source C backs this up because third and fourth graders lost ground in reading the first year. The Pinemont superintendent fixed it with tutoring, but that took extra effort and money. This is why I think a district must keep its hours up. Families also pay. Source B describes a parent paying 76 dollars a week for day care, and Source D says 41 percent of parents of young children had new childcare costs. Source E shows elementary parents are split, 48 percent to 42 percent, while local employers mostly want to go back, which shows that the people who feel the cost are not happy.

Some people might say the teacher hiring is more important than the childcare costs. That is a fair point, but a savings that just moves the cost to parents, as Source B says, is not really a savings. Pinemont Valley also says they "got lucky, and then we worked," so other districts should not assume it will go the same way for them.

In conclusion, a district should adopt the four-day week only with preserved hours, a funded Friday option for young children, and a plan to check the results. If it cannot do those things, it should keep five days and find another way to pay teachers.

annotations.comment: Clear conditional thesis with two named conditions (preserved hours, Friday care), so it earns the thesis point. The conditions are stated plainly and the essay stays consistent with them.

s-fb2-high-0.essay:
Most graduation speakers tell the audience they are ready. Marisol Quenneville, a night-shift charge nurse speaking to new nurses, has a harder job: she has to respect the four years of skills they just earned while telling them those skills are not what will matter most at three in the morning. She handles this by moving the graduates from a scene, to a story, to a statistic, and finally to a direct charge, and at each step she narrows what "attention" means until it is no longer a feeling but a habit they can perform. Most importantly, she concedes the exhaustion waiting for them so she can move the real danger somewhere they did not expect, from fatigue to certainty.

Quenneville opens with a sound instead of advice. The monitors "tick," the ice machine "groans," and a call light blinks "like a slow pulse." For an audience that has only done clinicals, this puts them on the floor before she asks anything of them, and the simile is telling, because even the background noise is given a heartbeat. Then she splits it: "Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything." Those two short sentences set up the problem the whole speech tries to solve, which is how to tell the difference. Only after that does she define her term, calling attention "a practice, like scrubbing in." This comparison is chosen for nurses specifically. Scrubbing in is something they have done hundreds of times no matter their mood, so she borrows a habit they already respect and attaches attention to it.

The story of the man in room 412 then shows what this practice looks like. Quenneville uses flat, repeated sentences, "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine," that sound like the reassuring data a tired nurse would accept. The repetition makes the twist hit harder: the only warning sign was a request to see the sky. She also admits she "nearly told him there was nothing out there but a parking lot," which matters because she isn't posing as a hero with perfect instincts. She was a third-year nurse, not far from where the graduates are now. Her conclusion, "I did not save him with a skill. I saved him by hearing a sentence," answers her own second paragraph: skills are what they learned in school, but hearing is what she is asking for now.

She knows the graduates will push back, so she lists their objections for them. The "fourteen clicks to record a glass of water" is specific enough to be funny, and it shows she hasn't forgotten what the job is like. Because she promises "I will not insult you by pretending otherwise," her rebuttal lands harder: the nurses who miss things "decided, somewhere along the way, that they already knew what they would find." The line "Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes" makes this memorable, but it is also a little uncomfortable for people who were just tested on knowing the answers. The confidence school rewarded is the "thief." Her hospital data backs this up, with forty-four of seventy-one rapid-response calls coming from a nurse who noticed "something was off," and repeating "Forty-four" alone forces the audience to sit with it. Still, she adds that machines "are good at what they measure." She is not telling them to ignore monitors, which would sound reckless with faculty in the room; she is telling them their job starts where the measuring stops.

By the last paragraph she has earned the right to give orders, and the tone shifts to imperatives: "stand still for three seconds," "Ask the second question." The request is concrete enough to try on a first shift. Her admission "I do not do it perfectly" keeps it from sounding like a lecture, and it actually supports her definition, since a discipline is something you never finish practicing. The ending brings back the opening scene: "The hall will be loud tonight and every night after. Listen anyway." The noise from the first paragraph hasn't gone away, and she doesn't pretend it will. Two words is all she leaves them with, which is about the right length for something to remember at three in the morning.

s-fb2-mid-0.essay:
In her commencement address, Marisol Quenneville wants the new nurses to see attention as a discipline and not a feeling, and she does this by using her own long experience to build trust and then using a story and a statistic to show that noticing people matters more than relying on machines. Because the graduates are proud of their technical skills, she has to convince them without insulting what they have learned.

She starts by describing the hospital at three in the morning, where "the monitors tick, the ice machine groans, somebody's call light blinks at the end of the hall like a slow pulse." This sensory detail puts the graduates in the place they are about to work, and the simile of the call light as a pulse makes the hospital seem alive. Then she says "Most of that noise means nothing. Some of it means everything." The short sentences set up the problem the rest of the speech is about, which is telling the difference. This is a good way to start because the graduates have never worked a night shift and she is showing them what it is like.

The most memorable part is the story of the man in room 412. Quenneville says his vitals were fine and his chart was fine, and then he asks her to open the blinds. The short sentences like "His vitals were fine. His chart was fine." sound calm and routine, which makes the moment when she asks "why" stand out. She ends with "I did not save him with a skill. I saved him by hearing a sentence." This is aimed right at the graduates, who just spent four years learning skills, and she is telling them that skill is not the whole job. The story makes her argument feel real instead of just an opinion.

Quenneville also admits the problems the graduates will face. She says they will have "six patients, sometimes eight" and be tired "in a way that has no name yet." By saying "I will not insult you by pretending otherwise" she shows she is being honest, so the audience is more likely to listen. Then she says "Fatigue takes your legs; certainty takes your eyes," which moves the danger from being busy to being sure of yourself. The metaphor of certainty as a thief makes it sound like something the graduates should be afraid of.

Next she uses the statistic that forty-four of seventy-one rapid-response calls came from nurses and not alarms. The one-word sentence "Forty-four" gives it emphasis. This proves that people notice things that machines do not, though she is careful to say she does not "disparage the machines."

At the end her tone changes to direct commands like "stand still for three seconds" and "Ask the second question." These are small, so the graduates can actually do them. She admits "I do not do it perfectly," which makes her seem human. The last line, "Listen anyway," is short and tells them to keep paying attention even when the hall is loud. Overall, Quenneville uses story, honesty, and evidence to persuade the graduates that attention is something they have to choose to practice.

s-fb3-high-0.essay:
Most of the fighting about car-free downtowns assumes there are only two choices: close the street or leave it alone. Marisol Teague's column about Carrow Street shows why that framing doesn't work. The hardware store owner, the baker, and the nurse are not just three opinions about cars. They are three different kinds of trips. A city should limit private cars downtown only on the blocks and during the hours when people come to stay, and it should keep car access wherever people come to fetch something heavy or have to leave after dark. How much a city restricts cars should depend on why people are on the street, not on one rule for all six blocks.

Start with the hardware store and the bakery, since they seem like opposites. The baker's customers come to linger. They buy a roll, sit down, maybe buy another, and Teague says they stay "because nothing is idling at their backs." For them the closed street is the product. The hardware customer is on an errand. Nobody lingers with a stack of two-by-fours, and nobody carries them eight blocks to a garage. So the closure costs the hardware store exactly the thing it sells, which is convenience. The fix is not to reopen the whole street. The city could put short loading bays at each end of the closed blocks, or let pickup trucks in before 9 a.m. on Saturdays. I'll admit this might not save every lumber sale. If the store is in the middle of the six blocks, a bay at the corner is still a long haul. In that case the honest answer is that some businesses don't fit a pedestrian block, and the city should either leave that one block open to slow traffic or help the store pay for delivery. Pretending the bakery's success makes up for the hardware store's loss is how the city ended up with a quarrel instead of a plan.

The nurse looks like the same complaint, but it isn't. Her problem has nothing to do with carrying anything. It's about time and safety. At eleven at night the bakery is closed and nobody is lingering, so the reason for closing the street is gone, but the closure is still pushing her eight blocks from her car. This is the easiest case to solve, because lingering happens at predictable hours. In my town, Main Street closes for the farmers market on Saturday mornings, and by one o'clock the barricades are gone and cars are parked at the curb again. Nobody fights about it, because the closure lines up with when people actually want to walk around. Carrow Street could do the same and reopen to cars at nine every night. Then the nurse isn't trading her safety for someone else's croissant.

Getting the degree wrong has consequences that reach past downtown. Teague mentions that the hardware customers now drive to "the outlet strip on the highway." If a city closes too much, it doesn't get rid of cars. It moves them, and it sorts people. Downtown ends up for people with free time and good legs, and everyone running errands, working night shifts, or unable to walk far gets sent to the highway. That's also why the right amount of restriction should change from city to city. A city with buses running late can close more, because the nurse has another way home. A small city like Verrick Falls, where the car is the only option for a lot of people, has to close less, and it has to close more carefully.

Teague says a downtown must be a place people can reach and a place people want to stay. Those two purposes don't really have to compete if the city stops treating the street as one thing. Close it when people are staying and open it when they need to reach it. The limits should be as big as the lingering and no bigger.

annotations.quote: A city should limit private cars downtown only on the blocks and during the hours when people come to stay, and it should keep car access wherever people come to fetch something heavy or have to leave after dark.
annotations.comment: This earns the thesis point. It takes a position on how far the limits should go, not just whether to have them, and it says what the degree depends on (blocks, hours, purpose of the trip). A reader could disagree with it.

annotations.quote: How much a city restricts cars should depend on why people are on the street, not on one rule for all six blocks.
annotations.comment: This states the principle the body paragraphs will use, so it sets up a line of reasoning and doesn't just repeat the prompt.

annotations.quote: So the closure costs the hardware store exactly the thing it sells, which is convenience.
annotations.comment: This is commentary, not summary. It explains why an errand business is hurt by a closure when a lingering business is helped, which ties the evidence to how much of the street to close.

annotations.quote: I'll admit this might not save every lumber sale. If the store is in the middle of the six blocks, a bay at the corner is still a long haul.
annotations.comment: The writer answers a counterexample to their own fix instead of just mentioning it, and offers alternatives (keep one block open, help pay for delivery).

annotations.quote: In my town, Main Street closes for the farmers market on Saturday mornings, and by one o'clock the barricades are gone
annotations.comment: Specific personal observation. It is used to show that lingering happens at predictable times, which supports the time-of-day rule.

annotations.quote: At eleven at night the bakery is closed and nobody is lingering, so the reason for closing the street is gone
annotations.comment: The nurse's situation is treated as a problem the position has to solve, and the writer applies their own reasoning to solve it. This is the kind of commentary that reaches the 4 level.

annotations.quote: The nurse looks like the same complaint, but it isn't. Her problem has nothing to do with carrying anything. It's about time and safety.
annotations.comment: The essay uses Teague's three people as a test for one principle and argues that the nurse and the hardware customer are different problems with different solutions. The rubric names this move as a way to earn sophistication.

annotations.quote: It moves them, and it sorts people.
annotations.comment: Puts the question in a wider context: who downtown is for, and what happens to the highway strip. This continues through the paragraph about transit.

annotations.quote: A city with buses running late can close more, because the nurse has another way home.
annotations.comment: The writer adjusts their position for different conditions (whether a city has transit), showing they have thought about unintended consequences of their own argument.

annotations.quote: The limits should be as big as the lingering and no bigger.
annotations.comment: A short, controlled closing line that sharpens the thesis instead of just decorating it.

s-fb3-mid-0.essay:
A city should limit private cars downtown only part of the time and only on the blocks where people mostly come to browse and eat, while keeping curbside access on the blocks where people come to carry things away. In other words, how much a city limits cars should depend on what each street is used for, not on one rule for the whole downtown.

The column about Verrick Falls shows why one rule does not work. The hardware store owner lost his Saturday customers because they used to park at the curb and load lumber, and now they drive to the outlet strip on the highway. You cannot carry lumber six blocks from a parking garage. This shows that a store that sells heavy things depends on cars, and if the city closes the street in front of it, the store loses business to the highway. The bakery owner has the opposite experience, since she sells more rolls when people can linger with nothing idling behind them. Bakeries and cafes sell a pleasant stop, so a quiet street helps them. So the closing of Carrow Street helped one business and hurt another, which means a city should look at what businesses are on a street before it closes it.

I have seen something like this in my own town. The street near my school with the coffee shops and the used bookstore has a farmers market on Sundays with the road blocked off, and it is always crowded and people seem happy. But the same weekend nobody would want the pharmacy two streets over to be blocked off, because older people drive there to pick up prescriptions and they cannot walk far. A closing that works for a market would not work for a pharmacy.

The nurse in the column is a harder problem. She gets off at eleven at night and has to walk eight blocks to the garage. I think the answer is time of day. The street can be closed during the day and on weekends when it is busy, and opened to cars at night so she can park close and feel safe. This costs the city something, because the street is less of a park at night, but there are few people lingering at that hour anyway, so the loss is small. Nobody is hurt much by letting cars back in at night, while the nurse could be hurt a lot.

Some people will say that any cars at all ruin a walkable downtown. But a downtown that nobody can reach is not walkable either, it is just empty. The best position is a middle one, with closures on the blocks and hours when lingering matters most, and cars allowed where people have to reach something. That way the city gets both purposes the column names, a place people can reach and a place they want to stay.

annotations.quote: A city should limit private cars downtown only part of the time and only on the blocks where people mostly come to browse and eat, while keeping curbside access on the blocks where people come to carry things away.
annotations.comment: Defensible, conditional thesis about the degree of limits (by time and by kind of block), not just whether cars exist. Earns the thesis point.

annotations.quote: You cannot carry lumber six blocks from a parking garage.
annotations.comment: Uses the hardware store from the column and gives a real mechanism (heavy goods need curb access), but this is mostly column material rather than new evidence.

annotations.quote: So the closing of Carrow Street helped one business and hurt another, which means a city should look at what businesses are on a street before it closes it.
annotations.comment: Links the two column examples back to the thesis, giving a followable line of reasoning, though the point is fairly general.

annotations.quote: A closing that works for a market would not work for a pharmacy.
annotations.comment: Personal example is specific enough to count, but the pharmacy is described briefly and the commentary is thin and repeats the earlier point about different businesses.

annotations.quote: I think the answer is time of day.
annotations.comment: Treats the nurse as a problem the position must solve, which is good, but the solution is stated simply and the claim that few people linger at night is asserted without support.

annotations.quote: But a downtown that nobody can reach is not walkable either, it is just empty.
annotations.comment: Brief rebuttal of the opposing view; it is a single sentence and the essay does not explore unintended consequences, so no sustained sophistication.

s-fb3-low-0.essay:
Cities have to decide how much to limit cars downtown and there are good points on both sides. In my opinion a city should limit cars but not too much, because downtowns need both cars and people walking.

In the column, Verrick Falls closed six blocks of Carrow Street and now people are arguing. The hardware store owner says his customers go to the highway now. The bakery lady says she sells more rolls. And the nurse is worried about walking to the garage at night. This shows that the issue is complicated because different people want different things. Some businesses like the closing and some do not.

I think that closing streets is good because people like to walk around. When there are no cars it is quieter and cleaner and people stay longer. Also it is safer for kids. A lot of cities have done this and it works for them. Studies show that walkable downtowns do better, so cities should do it more.

However, cars are important too. Not everybody can walk far, like old people or people who work late. If a city closes everything then people will just go somewhere else, like the outlet strip. That would hurt downtown. So a city should not close all of it.

In conclusion, a city should close some streets but leave some open for cars. This way the bakery and the hardware store can both be happy and the nurse can get to her car. It is a balance and each city has to find the right amount for them.

annotations.quote: a city should limit cars but not too much, because downtowns need both cars and people walking
annotations.comment: Takes a position, but 'not too much' is vague and the opening never says what the limit should depend on or where the line falls. This is close to restating the prompt's tension, so the thesis point is likely not earned.

annotations.quote: Cities have to decide how much to limit cars downtown and there are good points on both sides.
annotations.comment: Restates the prompt almost word for word and gestures at 'both sides' without committing to anything arguable.

annotations.quote: This shows that the issue is complicated because different people want different things.
annotations.comment: Summarizes the hardware owner, baker and nurse and concludes it is 'complicated' with no argument built from them. This is the level-1 pattern of listing the three figures.

annotations.quote: Studies show that walkable downtowns do better, so cities should do it more.
annotations.comment: Generic appeal to unnamed studies, with no specific example or explanation of the mechanism. This is the kind of generality that caps evidence at 1.

annotations.quote: A lot of cities have done this and it works for them.
annotations.comment: No city is named and no scene is described, so this is assertion rather than evidence. Commentary is absent.

annotations.quote: This way the bakery and the hardware store can both be happy and the nurse can get to her car.
annotations.comment: Proposes a compromise but never explains how leaving some streets open would serve each purpose, or why the hardware customer and the nurse are different problems. The compromise is not tested against the tension Teague names, so there is no sophistication.

annotations.quote: It is a balance and each city has to find the right amount for them.
annotations.comment: Falls back on 'it's a balance' and leaves the tension unresolved. This gestures at complexity without working through it.
